tasks.title: Rational Inequalities — 1
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{x - 2}{x + 1} \le 0$ is $-1 < x \le 2$.
The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{2x - 6}{x + 4} \ge 0$ is $(-\infty, -4) \cup [3, \infty)$.
The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{3x + 6}{x - 4} \le 0$ is $-2 \le x < 4$.
The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{x^{2} - 9}{x + 5} \ge 0$ is $(-5, -3] \cup [3, \infty)$.
The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{x + 5}{x - 3} \ge 0$ is $x \le -5$ or $x > 3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
\frac{x - 2}{x + 1}\le 0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

$$
x - 2=0\Rightarrow x=2
$$

$$
x + 1=0\Rightarrow x=-1
$$

(the pole $x=-1$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $\frac{x - 2}{x + 1}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,2)$ | $-$ |
| $(2,\infty)$ | $+$ |

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

$$
(-1, 2]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
\frac{2 x - 6}{x + 4}\ge 0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

$$
2 x - 6=0\Rightarrow x=3
$$

$$
x + 4=0\Rightarrow x=-4
$$

(the pole $x=-4$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $\frac{2 (x - 3)}{x + 4}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-4)$ | $+$ |
| $(-4,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

$$
(-\infty, -4) \cup [3, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
\frac{3 x + 6}{x - 4}\le 0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

$$
3 x + 6=0\Rightarrow x=-2
$$

$$
x - 4=0\Rightarrow x=4
$$

(the pole $x=4$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $\frac{3 (x + 2)}{x - 4}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-2)$ | $+$ |
| $(-2,4)$ | $-$ |
| $(4,\infty)$ | $+$ |

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

$$
[-2, 4)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
\frac{x^{2} - 9}{x + 5}\ge 0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

$$
x^{2} - 9=0\Rightarrow x=-3
$$

$$
x^{2} - 9=0\Rightarrow x=3
$$

$$
x + 5=0\Rightarrow x=-5
$$

(the pole $x=-5$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $\frac{x^{2} - 9}{x + 5}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-5)$ | $-$ |
| $(-5,-3)$ | $+$ |
| $(-3,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

$$
(-5, -3] \cup [3, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
\frac{x + 5}{x - 3}\ge 0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

$$

$$

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 2
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inequality $-4 \le x^{2} - 4x - 1 \le 4$ has solution set $[-1, 5]$.
The inequality $-1 \le x^{2} - 2x - 1 \le 3$ has solution set $[1 - \sqrt{5}, 1 + \sqrt{5}]$.
The inequality ${2 \le x^{2} - 2x + 3 \le 6}$ has solution set $[-1, 3]$.
The inequality $-4 \le x^{2} - 6x + 5 \le 5$ has solution set $[0, 6]$.
The inequality ${0 < x^{2} - 4x + 3 \le 3}$ has solution set $[0, 4]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
-4\le (x^{2} - 4 x) - 1\le 4
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
-4\le (x^{2} - 4 x) - 1
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x + 3\ge 0
$$

$$
(x - 3) (x - 1)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=1
$$

$$
x=3
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x + 3$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,1)$ | $+$ |
| $(1,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, 1] \cup [3, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 4 x) - 1\le 4
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x - 5\le 0
$$

$$
(x - 5) (x + 1)\le 0
$$

$$
x=-1
$$

$$
x=5
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x - 5$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,5)$ | $-$ |
| $(5,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
[-1, 5]
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
[-1, 1] \cup [3, 5]
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
-1\le (x^{2} - 2 x) - 1\le 3
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
-1\le (x^{2} - 2 x) - 1
$$

$$
x^{2} - 2 x\ge 0
$$

$$
x (x - 2)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=0
$$

$$
x=2
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x (x - 2)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,0)$ | $+$ |
| $(0,2)$ | $-$ |
| $(2,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, 0] \cup [2, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 2 x) - 1\le 3
$$

$$
x^{2} - 2 x - 4\le 0
$$

| $(1 - \sqrt{5},1 + \sqrt{5})$ | $-$ |
| $(1 + \sqrt{5},\infty)$ | $+$ |

$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$

$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inequality $-2 < x^{2} - 6x + 5 < 3$ has solution set $(3 - \sqrt{7}, 3 + \sqrt{7})$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x + 6} \ge x$ is $[-6, 3]$.
The solution set of the inequality $|x + 4| - |x - 2| \ge 3$ is $[0.5, \infty)$.
The inequality ${2 \le x^{2} - 4x + 5 \le 10}$ has solution set $[-1, 1] \cup [3, 5]$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x + 1} + \sqrt{x + 6} \le 5$ is $[-1, 3]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
-2<(x^{2} - 6 x) + 5<3
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
-2<(x^{2} - 6 x) + 5
$$

$$
x^{2} - 6 x + 7>0
$$

$$
x=3 - \sqrt{2}
$$

$$
x=\sqrt{2} + 3
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 6 x + 7$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,3 - \sqrt{2})$ | $+$ |
| $(3 - \sqrt{2},\sqrt{2} + 3)$ | $-$ |
| $(\sqrt{2} + 3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, 3 - \sqrt{2}) \cup (\sqrt{2} + 3, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 6 x) + 5<3
$$

$$
x^{2} - 6 x + 2<0
$$

$$
x=3 - \sqrt{7}
$$

$$
x=\sqrt{7} + 3
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 6 x + 2$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,3 - \sqrt{7})$ | $+$ |
| $(3 - \sqrt{7},\sqrt{7} + 3)$ | $-$ |
| $(\sqrt{7} + 3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
(3 - \sqrt{7}, \sqrt{7} + 3)
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
(3 - \sqrt{7}, 3 - \sqrt{2}) \cup (\sqrt{2} + 3, \sqrt{7} + 3)
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Start from the radical inequality.

$$
\sqrt{x + 6}\ge x
$$

Require every radicand to be nonnegative (domain).

$$
x + 6\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-6, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

A square root is always $\ge 0$, so the inequality holds automatically on the part of the domain where the right side is negative.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
x + 6\ge x^{2}
$$

$$
- x^{2} + x + 6\ge 0
$$

$$
- (x - 3) (x + 2)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=-2
$$

$$
x=3
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $- x^{2} + x + 6$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-2)$ | $-$ |
| $(-2,3)$ | $+$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $-$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$
[-6, 3]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Start from the absolute-value difference inequality.

$$
|x + 4|-|x - 2|\ge 3
$$

The expression changes formula at the kink points $x=-4$ and $x=2$.

On $x\le -4$:

$$
|x + 4|-|x - 2|=-6
$$

Solving $-6\ge 3$ on this piece gives

$$
\emptyset
$$

On $-4\le x\le 2$:

$$
|x + 4|-|x - 2|=2 x + 2
$$

Solving $2 x + 2\ge 3$ on this piece gives

$$
[\frac{1}{2}, 2]
$$

On $x\ge 2$:

$$
|x + 4|-|x - 2|=6
$$

Solving $6\ge 3$ on this piece gives

$$
[2, \infty)
$$

Union of the admissible pieces:

$$
[\frac{1}{2}, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
2\le (x^{2} - 4 x) + 5\le 10
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
2\le (x^{2} - 4 x) + 5
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x + 3\ge 0
$$

$$
(x - 3) (x - 1)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=1
$$

$$
x=3
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x + 3$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,1)$ | $+$ |
| $(1,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, 1] \cup [3, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 4 x) + 5\le 10
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x - 5\le 0
$$

$$
(x - 5) (x + 1)\le 0
$$

$$
x=-1
$$

$$
x=5
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x - 5$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,5)$ | $-$ |
| $(5,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
[-1, 5]
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
[-1, 1] \cup [3, 5]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Start from the two-radical inequality.

$$
\sqrt{x + 1}+\sqrt{x + 6}\le 5
$$

Require both radicands to be nonnegative.

$$
x + 1\ge 0
$$

$$
x + 6\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-1, \infty)
$$

Isolate one radical (right side must stay nonnegative), then square twice.

$$
\sqrt{x + 1}\le 5-\sqrt{x + 6}
$$

$$
\sqrt{x + 6}\le 5
$$

$$
x + 6\le 25
$$

After the first squaring, isolate the remaining radical and square again.

$$
2\cdot 5\sqrt{x + 6}\le 5^2+x + 6-x + 1
$$

Intersecting every domain and squared condition gives

$$
[-1, 3]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 21
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\bigl|\, |x - 5| - 2\bigr| \le 4$ is $[1, 9]$.

**A.** → False

Start from the absolute-value inequality.

$$
|{|{x - 5}| - 2}|\le 4
$$

An absolute value below a nonnegative constant unfolds to a compound inequality.

$$
-4\le |{x - 5}| - 2\le 4
$$

Solve the left half.

$$
|{x - 5}| - 2\ge -4
$$

$$
x\in \mathbb{R}
$$

Solve the right half.

$$
|{x - 5}| - 2\le 4
$$

$$
x\in [-1, 11]
$$

Intersect both halves.

$$
(-\infty, \infty)
$$

which does not match the claimed set $[1, 9]$.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
0<(x^{2} - 10 x) + 25\le 16
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
0<(x^{2} - 10 x) + 25
$$

$$
x^{2} - 10 x + 25>0
$$

$$
(x - 5)^{2}>0
$$

$$
x=5
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 10 x + 25$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,5)$ | $+$ |
| $(5,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, 5) \cup (5, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 10 x) + 25\le 16
$$

$$
x^{2} - 10 x + 9\le 0
$$

$$
(x - 9) (x - 1)\le 0
$$

$$
x=1
$$

$$
x=9
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 10 x + 9$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,1)$ | $+$ |
| $(1,9)$ | $-$ |
| $(9,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
[1, 9]
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
[1, 5) \cup (5, 9]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Start from the radical inequality.

$$
- \sqrt{2 x + 4} + \sqrt{5 x + 1}>1
$$

Require every radicand to be nonnegative (domain).

$$
2 x + 4\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-2, \infty)
$$

$$
5 x + 1\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [- \frac{1}{5}, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

A square root is always $\ge 0$, so the inequality holds automatically on the part of the domain where the right side is negative.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
7 x - 2 \sqrt{2 x + 4} \sqrt{5 x + 1} + 5>1
$$

$$
7 x - 2 \sqrt{2 x + 4} \sqrt{5 x + 1} + 4>0
$$

$$
7 x - 2 \sqrt{2} \sqrt{x + 2} \sqrt{5 x + 1} + 4>0
$$

$$
x=0
$$

$$
x=\frac{32}{9}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $7 x - 2 \sqrt{2} \sqrt{x + 2} \sqrt{5 x + 1} + 4$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,0)$ | $?$ |
| $(0,\frac{32}{9})$ | $-$ |
| $(\frac{32}{9},\infty)$ | $+$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$
(\frac{32}{9}, \infty)
$$

which does not match the claimed set $x \ge \frac{4}{3}$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Start from the absolute-value inequality.

$$
|{2 x - 5}|\ge |{3 x + 1}|
$$

Both sides are nonnegative absolute values, so squaring is equivalence-preserving.

$$
(2 x - 5)^{2}\ge (3 x + 1)^{2}
$$

$$
- 5 x^{2} - 26 x + 24\ge 0
$$

$$
- (x + 6) (5 x - 4)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=-6
$$

$$
x=\frac{4}{5}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $- 5 x^{2} - 26 x + 24$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-6)$ | $-$ |
| $(-6,\frac{4}{5})$ | $+$ |
| $(\frac{4}{5},\infty)$ | $-$ |

The solution set is

$$
[-6, \frac{4}{5}]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
2\le (x^{2} + 2 x) - 1<10
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
2\le (x^{2} + 2 x) - 1
$$

$$
x^{2} + 2 x - 3\ge 0
$$

$$
(x - 1) (x + 3)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=-3
$$

$$
x=1
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} + 2 x - 3$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-3)$ | $+$ |
| $(-3,1)$ | $-$ |
| $(1,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, -3] \cup [1, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} + 2 x) - 1<10
$$

$$
x^{2} + 2 x - 11<0
$$

$$
x=- 2 \sqrt{3} - 1
$$

$$
x=-1 + 2 \sqrt{3}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} + 2 x - 11$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,- 2 \sqrt{3} - 1)$ | $+$ |
| $(- 2 \sqrt{3} - 1,-1 + 2 \sqrt{3})$ | $-$ |
| $(-1 + 2 \sqrt{3},\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
(- 2 \sqrt{3} - 1, -1 + 2 \sqrt{3})
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
(- 2 \sqrt{3} - 1, -3] \cup [1, -1 + 2 \sqrt{3})
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

statements: The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{2x + 9} - \sqrt{x + 5} > 1$ is $x > -1 - 2\sqrt{3}$.

x\in [- \frac{9}{2}, \infty)
$$

$$
x + 5\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-5, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

A square root is always $\ge 0$, so the inequality holds automatically on the part of the domain where the right side is negative.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
3 x - 2 \sqrt{x + 5} \sqrt{2 x + 9} + 14>1
$$

$$
3 x - 2 \sqrt{x + 5} \sqrt{2 x + 9} + 13>0
$$

$$
3 x - 2 \sqrt{x + 5} \sqrt{2 x + 9} + 13>0

| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1 + 2 \sqrt{3})$ | $-$ |
| $(-1 + 2 \sqrt{3},\infty)$ | $+$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$

which does not match the claimed set $x > -1 - 2\sqrt{3}$.

**B.** → True

Start from the absolute-value inequality.

$$
|{(x^{2} - 4 x) - 1}|>4

An absolute value above a constant splits into two outer cases.

**Case 1.**

$$
(x^{2} - 4 x) - 1>4
$$

$$
x\in (-\infty, -1) \cup (5, \infty)
$$

**Case 2.**

$$
(x^{2} - 4 x) - 1<-4
$$

$$
x\in (1, 3)
$$

$$
(-\infty, -1) \cup (1, 3) \cup (5, \infty)
$$

**C.** → False

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
-6\le (x^{2} - 4 x) - 3<5

$$
-6\le (x^{2} - 4 x) - 3
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x + 3\ge 0
$$

$$
(x - 3) (x - 1)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=1
$$

$$
x=3
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x + 3$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,1)$ | $+$ |
| $(1,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, 1] \cup [3, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 4 x) - 3<5
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x - 8<0
$$

$$
x=2 - 2 \sqrt{3}
$$

$$
x=2 + 2 \sqrt{3}
$$

| --- | --- |

| $(2 - 2 \sqrt{3},2 + 2 \sqrt{3})$ | $-$ |

which does not match the claim.

**D.** → True

Start from the radical inequality.

$$

Require every radicand to be nonnegative (domain).

$$
x + 3\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-3, \infty)
$$

If the right side is negative, a nonnegative square root cannot lie strictly below it; only the boundary $0$ can matter for non-strict inequalities.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
x + 3<x^{2} - 2 x + 1
$$

$$
- x^{2} + 3 x + 2<0
$$

$$

$$

$$
x=\frac{3}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}
$$

| --- | --- |

**E.** → True

Start from the absolute-value sum inequality.

$$
|x + 2|+|x - 5|=3 - 2 x

$$
[- \frac{7}{2}, -2]

$$
[-2, 5]

$$

$$

Solving $2 x - 3\le 10$ on this piece gives

$$
[5, \frac{13}{2}]
$$

Union of the admissible pieces:

$$
[- \frac{7}{2}, \frac{13}{2}]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

| $(1,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

(-\infty, 1) \cup (1, \infty)

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 2 x) - 2<6

$$
x^{2} - 2 x - 8<0
$$

$$
(x - 4) (x + 2)<0
$$

$$
x=-2
$$

$$
x=4
$$

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 2 x - 8$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-2)$ | $+$ |
| $(-2,4)$ | $-$ |
| $(4,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
(-2, 4)
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
(-2, 1) \cup (1, 4)
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 24
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x^{2} - 4x - 5} \le x + 2$ is $[\frac{-9}{8}, -1] \cup [5, \infty)$.
The solution set of the inequality $|x - 3| - |x + 1| \ge -2$ is $(-\infty, 2)$.
The inequality ${3 < x^{2} + 2x - 1 < 11}$ has solution set $(-1 - \sqrt{13}, -1 - \sqrt{5}) \cup (-1 + \sqrt{5}, -1 + \sqrt{13})$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x + 3} + \sqrt{x + 8} \le 5$ is $[-3, 1]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Start from the radical inequality.

$$
\sqrt{(x^{2} - 4 x) - 5}\le x + 2
$$

Require every radicand to be nonnegative (domain).

$$
x^{2} - 4 x - 5\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in (-\infty, -1] \cup [5, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

If the right side is negative, a nonnegative square root cannot lie strictly below it; only the boundary $0$ can matter for non-strict inequalities.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
x^{2} - 4 x - 5\le x^{2} + 4 x + 4
$$

$$
- 8 x - 9\le 0
$$

$$
x=- \frac{9}{8}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $- 8 x - 9$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,- \frac{9}{8})$ | $+$ |
| $(- \frac{9}{8},\infty)$ | $-$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$
[- \frac{9}{8}, -1] \cup [5, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Start from the absolute-value difference inequality.

$$
|x - 3|-|x + 1|\ge -2
$$

The expression changes formula at the kink points $x=-1$ and $x=3$.

On $x\le -1$:

$$
|x - 3|-|x + 1|=4
$$

Solving $4\ge -2$ on this piece gives

$$
(-\infty, -1]
$$

On $-1\le x\le 3$:

$$
|x - 3|-|x + 1|=2 - 2 x
$$

Solving $2 - 2 x\ge -2$ on this piece gives

$$
[-1, 2]
$$

On $x\ge 3$:

$$
|x - 3|-|x + 1|=-4
$$

Solving $-4\ge -2$ on this piece gives

$$
\emptyset
$$

Union of the admissible pieces:

$$
(-\infty, 2]
$$

which does not match the claimed set $(-\infty, 2)$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
3<(x^{2} + 2 x) - 1<11
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
3<(x^{2} + 2 x) - 1
$$

$$
x^{2} + 2 x - 4>0
$$

$$
x=- \sqrt{5} - 1
$$

$$
x=-1 + \sqrt{5}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} + 2 x - 4$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,- \sqrt{5} - 1)$ | $+$ |
| $(- \sqrt{5} - 1,-1 + \sqrt{5})$ | $-$ |
| $(-1 + \sqrt{5},\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, - \sqrt{5} - 1) \cup (-1 + \sqrt{5}, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} + 2 x) - 1<11
$$

$$
x^{2} + 2 x - 12<0
$$

$$
x=- \sqrt{13} - 1
$$

$$
x=-1 + \sqrt{13}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} + 2 x - 12$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,- \sqrt{13} - 1)$ | $+$ |
| $(- \sqrt{13} - 1,-1 + \sqrt{13})$ | $-$ |
| $(-1 + \sqrt{13},\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
(- \sqrt{13} - 1, -1 + \sqrt{13})
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
(- \sqrt{13} - 1, - \sqrt{5} - 1) \cup (-1 + \sqrt{5}, -1 + \sqrt{13})
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Start from the two-radical inequality.

$$
\sqrt{x + 3}+\sqrt{x + 8}\le 5
$$

Require both radicands to be nonnegative.

$$
x + 3\ge 0
$$

$$
x + 8\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-3, \infty)
$$

Isolate one radical (right side must stay nonnegative), then square twice.

$$
\sqrt{x + 3}\le 5-\sqrt{x + 8}
$$

$$
\sqrt{x + 8}\le 5
$$

$$
x + 8\le 25
$$

After the first squaring, isolate the remaining radical and square again.

$$
2\cdot 5\sqrt{x + 8}\le 5^2+x + 8-x + 3
$$

Intersecting every domain and squared condition gives

$$
[-3, 1]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 25
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\bigl|\, |x + 3| - 5\bigr| < 4$ is $(-12, -4) \cup (-2, 6)$.
The inequality ${0 < x^{2} + 2x + 1 \le 9}$ has solution set $[-4, 2]$.

**A.** → True

Start from the absolute-value inequality.

$$
|{|{x + 3}| - 5}|<4
$$

An absolute value below a nonnegative constant unfolds to a compound inequality.

$$
-4<|{x + 3}| - 5<4
$$

Solve the left half.

$$
|{x + 3}| - 5>-4
$$

$$
x\in (-\infty, -4) \cup (-2, \infty)
$$

Solve the right half.

$$
|{x + 3}| - 5<4
$$

$$
x\in (-12, 6)
$$

Intersect both halves.

$$
(-12, -4) \cup (-2, 6)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
0<(x^{2} + 2 x) + 1\le 9
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
0<(x^{2} + 2 x) + 1
$$

$$
(x^{2} + 2 x) + 1>0
$$

$$
(x + 1)^{2}>0
$$

$$
x=-1
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x (x + 2) + 1$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, -1) \cup (-1, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} + 2 x) + 1\le 9
$$

$$
x^{2} + 2 x - 8\le 0
$$

$$
(x - 2) (x + 4)\le 0
$$

$$
x=-4
$$

$$
x=2
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} + 2 x - 8$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-4)$ | $+$ |
| $(-4,2)$ | $-$ |
| $(2,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
[-4, 2]
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
[-4, -1) \cup (-1, 2]
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Start from the radical inequality.

$$
- \sqrt{x + 2} + \sqrt{3 x + 10}>2
$$

Require every radicand to be nonnegative (domain).

$$
3 x + 10\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [- \frac{10}{3}, \infty)
$$

$$
x + 2\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-2, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

A square root is always $\ge 0$, so the inequality holds automatically on the part of the domain where the right side is negative.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
4 x - 2 \sqrt{x + 2} \sqrt{3 x + 10} + 12>4
$$

$$
4 x - 2 \sqrt{x + 2} \sqrt{3 x + 10} + 8>0
$$

$$
2 (2 x - \sqrt{x + 2} \sqrt{3 x + 10} + 4)>0
$$

$$
x=-2
$$

$$
x=2
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $2 (2 x - \sqrt{x + 2} \sqrt{3 x + 10} + 4)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-2)$ | $?$ |
| $(-2,2)$ | $-$ |
| $(2,\infty)$ | $+$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$
(2, \infty)
$$

which does not match the claimed set $x \ge -2$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Start from the absolute-value inequality.

$$
|{5 x + 2}|\ge |{2 x - 9}|
$$

Both sides are nonnegative absolute values, so squaring is equivalence-preserving.

$$
(5 x + 2)^{2}\ge (2 x - 9)^{2}
$$

$$
21 x^{2} + 56 x - 77\ge 0
$$

$$
7 (x - 1) (3 x + 11)\ge 0
$$

$$
x=- \frac{11}{3}
$$

$$
x=1
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $7 (3 x^{2} + 8 x - 11)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,- \frac{11}{3})$ | $+$ |
| $(- \frac{11}{3},1)$ | $-$ |
| $(1,\infty)$ | $+$ |

The solution set is

$$
(-\infty, - \frac{11}{3}] \cup [1, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 26
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inequality $-2 \le x^{2} - 4x - 1 < 7$ has solution set $(2 - 2\sqrt{3}, 2 - \sqrt{3}] \cup [2 + \sqrt{3}, 2 + 2\sqrt{3})$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{2x + 3} < \sqrt{5x + 4} - 1$ is $x > \dfrac{4 - 2\sqrt{31}}{9}$.

The inequality $-7 \le x^{2} - 2x - 6 < 3$ has solution set $(1 - \sqrt{10}, 1 + \sqrt{10})$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
-2\le (x^{2} - 4 x) - 1<7
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
-2\le (x^{2} - 4 x) - 1
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x + 1\ge 0
$$

$$
x=2 - \sqrt{3}
$$

$$
x=\sqrt{3} + 2
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x + 1$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,2 - \sqrt{3})$ | $+$ |
| $(2 - \sqrt{3},\sqrt{3} + 2)$ | $-$ |
| $(\sqrt{3} + 2,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, 2 - \sqrt{3}] \cup [\sqrt{3} + 2, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 4 x) - 1<7
$$

$$
x^{2} - 4 x - 8<0
$$

$$
x=2 - 2 \sqrt{3}
$$

$$
x=2 + 2 \sqrt{3}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x - 8$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,2 - 2 \sqrt{3})$ | $+$ |
| $(2 - 2 \sqrt{3},2 + 2 \sqrt{3})$ | $-$ |
| $(2 + 2 \sqrt{3},\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
(2 - 2 \sqrt{3}, 2 + 2 \sqrt{3})
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
(2 - 2 \sqrt{3}, 2 - \sqrt{3}] \cup [\sqrt{3} + 2, 2 + 2 \sqrt{3})
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Start from the radical inequality.

$$
\sqrt{2 x + 3}<\sqrt{5 x + 4} - 1
$$

Require every radicand to be nonnegative (domain).

$$
5 x + 4\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [- \frac{4}{5}, \infty)
$$

$$
2 x + 3\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [- \frac{3}{2}, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

If the right side is negative, a nonnegative square root cannot lie strictly below it; only the boundary $0$ can matter for non-strict inequalities.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
2 x + 3<5 x - 2 \sqrt{5 x + 4} + 5
$$

$$
- 3 x + 2 \sqrt{5 x + 4} - 2<0
$$

$$
- 3 x + 2 \sqrt{5 x + 4} - 2<0
$$

$$
x=\frac{4}{9} + \frac{2 \sqrt{31}}{9}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $- 3 x + 2 \sqrt{5 x + 4} - 2$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,\frac{4}{9} + \frac{2 \sqrt{31}}{9})$ | $+$ |
| $(\frac{4}{9} + \frac{2 \sqrt{31}}{9},\infty)$ | $-$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$
(\frac{4}{9} + \frac{2 \sqrt{31}}{9}, \infty)
$$

which does not match the claimed set $x > \dfrac{4 - 2\sqrt{31}}{9}$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Start from the absolute-value inequality.

$$
|{(x^{2} + x) - 5}|>7
$$

An absolute value above a constant splits into two outer cases.

**Case 1.**

$$
(x^{2} + x) - 5>7
$$

$$
x\in (-\infty, -4) \cup (3, \infty)
$$

**Case 2.**

$$
(x^{2} + x) - 5<-7
$$

$$
x\in \emptyset
$$

Union of the two cases:

$$
(-\infty, -4) \cup (3, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
-7\le (x^{2} - 2 x) - 6<3
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
-7\le (x^{2} - 2 x) - 6
$$

$$
x^{2} - 2 x + 1\ge 0
$$

$$
(x - 1)^{2}\ge 0
$$

$$
x=1
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 2 x + 1$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,1)$ | $+$ |
| $(1,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 2 x) - 6<3
$$

$$
x^{2} - 2 x - 9<0
$$

$$
x=1 - \sqrt{10}
$$

$$
x=1 + \sqrt{10}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 2 x - 9$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,1 - \sqrt{10})$ | $+$ |
| $(1 - \sqrt{10},1 + \sqrt{10})$ | $-$ |
| $(1 + \sqrt{10},\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
(1 - \sqrt{10}, 1 + \sqrt{10})
$$

Intersect both pieces.

$$
(1 - \sqrt{10}, 1 + \sqrt{10})
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

$$

$$

tasks.context: A store applies a 20% discount to an item's original price p, then adds 8% sales tax on the discounted price, then subtracts a flat \$5 loyalty coupon at the very end. The final price is ${0.8p \times 1.08 - 5 = 0.864p - 5}$. A customer wants the final price to be \$70 or less.

The maximum original price, to the nearest whole dollar, that keeps the final price at or under \$70 is \$86.

**A.** → True

The final-price model is

$$
0.864p-5
$$

Substitute $p=86$.

$$
0.864(86)-5=69.304
$$

$$
69.304\le 70
$$

so an original price of 86 keeps the final price at or under 70.

**B.** → False

Translate the claim into arithmetic and unwind every step.

The final-price model is

$$
0.864p-5
$$

$$
0.864(87)-5=70.168
$$

$$
70.168\le 70
$$

is false, so 87 does not keep the final price at or under 70.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

$$
0.864p-5\le 70
$$

$$
0.864p\le 75
$$

$$
p\le \frac{75}{0.864}=86.805\ldots
$$

The largest whole-dollar original price is therefore 86.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

$$
0.8p(1.08)-5=0.864p-5
$$

$$
(p-5)(0.8)(1.08)=0.864p-4.32
$$

Each substitution and rearrangement above is written as its own display line.

Comparing the final numeric or inequality result with the claim shows a contradiction.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Translate the claim into arithmetic and unwind every step.

Apply discount, then tax, then the flat coupon.

$$
0.8p\times 1.08-5
$$

$$
0.864p-5
$$

which is exactly the claimed combined formula.

So the statement is True.

Producing 45 units exceeds this maximum.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Start from the radical inequality.

$$
\sqrt{3 x + 1}\le 2 x - 1
$$

Require every radicand to be nonnegative (domain).

$$
3 x + 1\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [- \frac{1}{3}, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

If the right side is negative, a nonnegative square root cannot lie strictly below it; only the boundary $0$ can matter for non-strict inequalities.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
3 x + 1\le 4 x^{2} - 4 x + 1
$$

$$
- 4 x^{2} + 7 x\le 0
$$

$$
- x (4 x - 7)\le 0
$$

$$
x=0
$$

$$
x=\frac{7}{4}
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x (7 - 4 x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,0)$ | $-$ |
| $(0,\frac{7}{4})$ | $+$ |
| $(\frac{7}{4},\infty)$ | $-$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$
[\frac{7}{4}, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
